## Day 109: β, learning rate and forgetting in DPO
**Review today:** Day 108 (+1), Day 106 (+3), Day 102 (+7), Day 88 (+21; quick 15-min skim of its self-check).

### Block 1: Concept lesson (1h15)
**β in DPO.** In the RLHF objective β is the KL weight. In the DPO loss it is the scale on log-ratios inside the sigmoid. Larger β means a given log-prob change produces a bigger margin, so the loss saturates *sooner* and the gradient weight σ(−margin) drops sooner. The policy therefore moves less from π_ref. Smaller β lets the policy move further before the loss is satisfied. That is the same direction as in Day 106: big β = stay close.

**Learning rate interacts.** With LoRA at lr 5e-4 (Day 108) the optimiser can satisfy the loss in a few steps by drastic changes. Lower lr changes the path, no

t only the speed: a small step size finds changes closer to the reference.

**Forgetting.** Preference tuning can damage abilities that the pairs do not cover. A cheap proxy is perplexity on held-out general text. We reuse Week 15's Shakespeare validation text: 8 windows of 256 tokens, on which the instruct model scored 32.05 (Week 15 log `day104_eval_finetuned.log`).

**Measuring movement.** Three numbers tell you how far the policy moved: Δlog-prob of chosen and rejected on held-out pairs, the change in general perplexity, and sample outputs. A full KL estimate would require sampling from the policy; Δlog-probs on the pairs are a cheap substitute.

### Block 2: Worked example (45 min)
`code/week-16/day109_dpo_sweep.py` reruns `day108_dpo.py` with lr 1e-4, 60 steps × 4 pairs, and β ∈ {0.1

, 0.5}, and adds the Shakespeare perplexity.

**Verified (out/day109_dpo_sweep.log):**

| Setting | Held-out margin | Δ chosen | Δ rejected | Exact match | Shakespeare ppl | Example output |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Day 108: β 0.1, lr 5e-4, 120 steps | 13.53 | +8.6 | −126.7 | 0.17 | not measured | "clouds orange springfirehose" |
| β 0.1, lr 1e-4, 60 steps | 9.19 | +10.7 | −81.2 | 0.23 | 32.35 | "clouds orange spring" |
| β 0.5, lr 1e-4, 60 steps | 11.32 | +12.3 | −10.3 | 0.20 | 32.14 | "cloud orange lemon spring" |

Both lr 1e-4 runs trained in 35-36 s and reached held-out preference accuracy 1.00. With β = 0.5 the rejected answer moved only −10.3 nats instead of −81.2, exactly the "stay closer" effect, and the example output keeps all four words (wrong order, but well-formed). Per

plexity barely moved from 32.05 in either case (32.35 and 32.14), so on this proxy neither run forgot much. Exact match is 0.20-0.23 on 40 prompts; Day 110 shows that such differences are within noise.

## Day 110: LLM evaluation pitfalls
**Review today:** Day 109 (+1), Day 107 (+3), Day 103 (+7), Day 89 (+21; quick 15-min skim of its self-check).

### Block 1: Concept lesson (1h15)
An evaluation number is a measurement with error bars and assumptions. Six pitfalls cause most bad conclusions.

**1. Small samples.** With n test items and accuracy p, the standard error is about √(p(1−p)/n). On 40 items at p = 0.2 that is about 0.06, so differences of 0.03-0.06 are noise. Report a confidence interval; the bootstrap (resample the per-item results with replacement many times) is simple and assumption-light.

**2. Prompt sensitivity.** Small models, and sometimes large ones, change their answers when the instruction is reworded, the casing changes or punctuation is removed. One prompt template

is one sample from a distribution of reasonable prompts. Report several, or fix the template and say so.

**3. Metric choice.** Exact match, normalised match (lowercase, strip punctuation) and "contains the answer" can give different numbers for the same outputs. "Contains" can reward a model that outputs many candidates. Choose the metric before looking at results and report how it was computed.

**4. Contamination.** If test items (or close variants) appear in training data, scores measure memorisation. Check exact overlap and n-gram overlap. For public benchmarks and web-trained models you usually *cannot* fully check, which is why fresh, private or dynamically generated tests matter.

**5. Judge bias.** LLM judges have position, length and self-preference biases. Week 15 measured this:

the 135M instruct judge gave 0 of 16 consistent verdicts when the two answers were swapped.

**6. Optimising the metric.** Once a number is a target, models and people tune toward it (Goodhart's law). The Day 107 RM shortcut and the Day 111 reward exploitation are versions of this.

| "reverse the order of these words …" (lowercase, no colon) | 0.07 | 0.07 | 0.07 |

0.12 |

- Contamination: 0/40 test prompts appear in training; 0/40 test word *sets* appear in training in another order.

## Day 111: Best-of-n, verifiers and exploiting an implicit reward
**Review today:** Day 110 (+1), Day 108 (+3), Day 104 (+7), Day 90 (+21; quick 15-min skim of its self-check).

### Block 1: Concept lesson (1h15)
**Best-of-n (rejection sampling).** Sample n answers, score each, return the best. It is the simplest way to "optimise" against a reward without changing weights. Its strength depends on two things: whether the right answer appears among the samples at all (*pass@n*), and whether the scorer can recognise it.

**Scorers.** (a) The policy's own log-prob: picks the answer the model already likes most; close to greedy. (b) A learned reward model: works if the RM is accurate on these samples. (c) A *verifier*: for tasks with checkable answers (unit tests, exact arithmetic, word revers

al) a program can decide correctness. With a perfect verifier, best-of-n accuracy equals pass@n.

**DPO's implicit reward as a scorer.** DPO defines r̂(x,y) = β·log(π_θ(y|x)/π_ref(y|x)). It looks like a free reward model. But it was only trained to rank the chosen/rejected kinds of answers. On other samples, especially strange ones the reference finds very unlikely, the ratio can be huge for a bad answer. That is reward hacking at inference time.

**Best-of-n and RLHF.** Best-of-n is also used to build training data (keep the best samples and fine-tune on them: "rejection sampling fine-tuning", or "expert iteration"), and as a baseline: an RL method should beat best-of-n at the same compute.

### Block 2: Worked example (45 min)
`code/week-16/day111_best_of_n.py`: for each of the 40 test p

rompts, sample 8 answers from the Day 108 DPO model at temperature 0.8 and choose by each scorer. The implicit reward uses β = 0.1; the reference log-probs come from the same model with the LoRA scale set to 0. Run time 54 s.

**Verified (out/day111_best_of_n.log):**
- Greedy: 0.17.
- Best-of-8 by policy log-prob: 0.15.
- Best-of-8 by DPO implicit reward: **0.00**.
- Oracle verifier (pass@8): 0.20.
- Mean distinct samples per prompt: 5.4 of 8.

The verifier gains only a little over greedy (0.17 → 0.20), because the correct answer rarely appears among 8 samples: this policy is weak, so selection cannot help much. Choosing by the implicit reward never picked a correct answer, even on prompts where the verifier found one among the samples (random choice was not measured). The samples it picks

are ones the reference model finds extremely unlikely, which the log-ratio rewards. A scorer outside its training distribution is exploited by optimisation, even one as mild as picking 1 of 8.

### Block 3: Lab (2h)

### Block 4: Practice (1h)
1. Why can best-of-n with a perfect verifier never exceed pass@

n?
2. Why might choosing by the policy's log-prob (0.15) be slightly below greedy (0.17)?
3. Why is the DPO implicit reward exploitable on samples it never saw?
4. Name two tasks where verifiers exist and two where they do not.

**Answers.** (1) It can only return one of the samples; if none is correct, nothing is. (2) Sampling at temperature 0.8 may not include the greedy answer, and the highest-probability *sample* is not always the greedy sequence; with n = 40 the 0.02 gap is one item, i.e. noise. (3) It is a log-ratio; any answer the reference rates very unlikely gets a big value if the policy rates it less unlikely, whether or not it is good. (4) Verifiable: code with tests, maths with known answers. Not verifiable: essay quality, helpfulness of advice.

### Extra notes
Best-of-n has a cost (n generations per query) and a well-known analytic KL to the base policy, which grows only like log n. That makes it a useful reference point when comparing RL methods. Verifier-based methods (reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards) are a major current direction exactly because verifiers do not drift like learned RMs; but they exist only for some tasks.

- Reporting pass@n as if it were single-answer accuracy.
- Forgetting the n× inference cost.

**The question.** Given preference pairs, is it better to (a) do SFT on the chosen answers only, (b) do DPO, or (c) do DPO plus an NLL (SFT) term on the chosen answer? Option (c) is a common fix for DPO lowering the chosen likelihood: the NLL term explicitly keeps the chosen answer probable.

## Day 113: Embeddings, chunking and vector search
**Review today:** Day 112 (+1), Day 110 (+3), Day 106 (+7), Day 92 (+21; quick 15-min skim of its self-check).

### Block 1: Concept lesson (1h15)
**Why retrieval?** A language model only knows what is in its weights, frozen at training time, and small models know little. Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) fetches relevant text at query time and puts it in the prompt. It lets a model use private, recent or large documents without retraining, and it makes answers checkable against a source.

**Sentence embeddings.** An embedding model maps a text to a vector so that texts with similar meaning are close. MiniLM-L6 produces 384-dimensional vectors: run the encoder, average the token vectors weighted by the attention mask (*mean pooling*), a

nd L2-normalise. With unit vectors, cosine similarity is just a dot product. These models are trained contrastively on (query, relevant passage) pairs, so "close" means "likely relevant", not "same words".

**Chunking.** Documents are too long to embed as one vector (MiniLM is used with at most 256 tokens here, and longer input is truncated), and one vector for a whole document blurs its topics. So we split into *chunks*. Trade-offs:
- Small chunks are precise but may lose context ("it" without the noun).
- Large chunks keep context but dilute the vector and cost more prompt tokens; beyond the model's limit they are silently truncated.
- *Overlap* between consecutive windows avoids cutting an idea in half.
- *Structure-aware* chunking (by heading or section) follows the author's own bounda

ries.
Prepending the document title ("Day 108 DPO from scratch: …") to each chunk is a cheap way to keep context.

**Vector search.** With N chunks and d dimensions, exact (brute-force) search is a matrix product: N·d multiply-adds per query. For a few thousand chunks that is microseconds. Approximate nearest-neighbour indexes (HNSW graphs, IVF clustering, product quantisation) matter at millions of vectors, trading a little recall for speed and memory.

**Evaluating retrieval.** Recall@k: is a relevant chunk among the top k? MRR (mean reciprocal rank): average of 1/rank of the first relevant chunk. You need queries with known relevant documents; here they come from the notes' own interview questions.

### Block 2: Worked example (45 min)
`code/week-17/day113_embed_search.py` parses the no

tes into 112 days, extracts 58 queries and compares four chunkings. Example query: "Why not train ten separate yes/no classifiers instead of one softmax model?" → gold day 34.

**Verified (out/day113_embed_search.log):**

| Chunking | Chunks | Embed time | recall@1 | recall@5 | MRR |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 64 words, overlap 16 | 2,012 | 18.3 s | 0.43 | 0.62 | 0.52 |
| 128 words, overlap 32 | 1,037 | 14.5 s | 0.40 | 0.64 | 0.51 |
| 256 words, overlap 64 | 550 | 4.7 s | 0.34 | 0.64 | 0.50 |
| by section | 1,099 | 9.4 s | 0.40 | **0.71** | **0.54** |

- Searching all 58 queries took 0.4-1.5 ms in total (brute force).
- The 128-word index is 1.59 MB in fp32 and 0.40 MB as int8 (per-vector scale); int8 retrieval gave recall@1 0.40, recall@5 0.62, MRR 0.51, almost the same as fp32.

Reading

With 58 queries a difference of 0.03 is about two queries, so only the larger gaps mean anything (Day 110).

## Day 114: Hybrid retrieval, reranking and retrieval evaluation
**Review today:** Day 113 (+1), Day 111 (+3), Day 107 (+7), Day 93 (+21; quick 15-min skim of its self-check).

### Block 1: Concept lesson (1h15)
**Lexical retrieval: BM25.** BM25 scores a document by the query terms it contains, weighted by inverse document frequency (rare words count more), with term frequency saturating (parameter k1) and a length normalisation (parameter b). It needs no training, is fast, and is very good at exact names, numbers, code identifiers and rare terms, which dense models can blur.

**Dense retrieval** (Day 113) is good at paraphrase and meaning, worse at exact rare tokens. The two make *different* errors, which is why combining them helps.

**Hybrid by reciprocal rank fusion (RRF).** Score each

document by Σ over retrievers of 1/(k + rank), with k ≈ 60. RRF uses only ranks, so you do not need to calibrate BM25 scores against cosine similarities.

**Reranking.** A *bi-encoder* embeds query and document separately, so documents can be pre-computed. A *cross-encoder* reads query and document *together* through one transformer and outputs a relevance score. It is much more accurate, because every query token can attend to every document token, but it must run once per (query, candidate) pair, so it is only used on the top 20-100 candidates from a cheaper first stage. This two-stage pattern (recall-oriented retrieval, then precision-oriented reranking) is standard.

**Evaluation discipline.** Keep the query set fixed, report recall@k and MRR at the k you will actually put in the prom

pt, report latency per query, and look at failures by hand.

### Block 2: Worked example (45 min)
`code/week-17/day114_hybrid_rerank.py` uses the 128/32 index from Day 113 (1,037 chunks).

**Verified (out/day114_hybrid_rerank.log):**

| Retriever | recall@1 | recall@5 | MRR | Cost |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Dense (MiniLM) | 0.40 | 0.64 | 0.51 | |
| BM25 | 0.41 | 0.67 | 0.51 | index + scoring all 58 queries 0.1 s |
| Hybrid RRF | 0.41 | 0.76 | 0.56 | |
| Dense top-20 + cross-encoder | **0.50** | **0.81** | **0.63** | 200 ms/query |
| Hybrid top-20 + cross-encoder | 0.48 | 0.79 | 0.62 | 213 ms/query |

Reading: on these notes, simple BM25 was as good as dense retrieval (0.67 vs 0.64 recall@5). Fusion raised recall@5 to 0.76 because the two retrievers miss different queries. The cross-encoder

added the most: recall@1 0.40 → 0.50. After reranking, dense and hybrid first stages ended within one or two queries of each other (0.81 vs 0.79), which is noise at n = 58. The price is latency: about 200 ms per query on this CPU for 20 pairs.

## Day 115: RAG generation and grounding evaluation
**Review today:** Day 114 (+1), Day 112 (+3), Day 108 (+7), Day 94 (+21; quick 15-min skim of its self-check).

### Block 1: Concept lesson (1h15)
**The RAG prompt.** Retrieve the top k chunks, put them in the prompt with clear separators and an instruction ("Answer using only the context. If the answer is not there, say you don't know."), then ask the question. Design choices: k (more context raises recall but costs tokens and can distract a small model), the order of chunks, whether to cite chunk ids, and the chat template (Week 15).

**Two failure modes.** A wrong RAG answer is either a *retrieval* failure (the needed text was not in the prompt) or a *generation* failure (it was there, but the model ignored, misread or contradicted it)

. Measure them separately:
- *Context recall*: fraction of questions whose answer string appears in the retrieved context.
- *Answer accuracy*: fraction of answers containing the gold answer.
- *Faithfulness / grounding*: whether claims in the answer are supported by the context. With short factual answers, a string check is a crude proxy; LLM judges and human checks are more general (Day 110 warns about judge biases).

**Baselines.** Always compare with *closed-book* (no context: what does the model already know?) and an *oracle* (give the passage known to contain the answer: what does perfect retrieval buy?). The gap closed-book → RAG is the value of retrieval; the gap RAG → oracle is retrieval's remaining error; oracle's own score is the generator's ceiling.

### Block 2: Worked example

(45 min)
`code/week-17/day115_rag_generate.py` uses the hybrid retriever with reranking, top 3 chunks, SmolLM2-135M-Instruct, greedy decoding, and 12 questions whose answers are numbers or short phrases from Weeks 15-16 (all 12 answer strings were confirmed present in the notes).

**Verified (out/day115_rag_generate.log):**
- Context recall@3: **0.92** (11 of 12 questions had the answer in the context).
- Accuracy: closed-book **0.00**, RAG **0.25**, "oracle" passage **0.08**.
- Mean RAG prompt length: 816 tokens. Whole run: 30 s.
- Typical failures with the right context present: an answer of "192 perplexity" for a different value, and "2 trainable parameters" for a question whose answer in the context was 2,442,817.

Reading: retrieval worked (0.92) but the 135M generator could not reli

ably copy facts from an 816-token prompt. The "oracle" scored *below* RAG because our oracle is crude: the first chunk containing the answer string, which may mention the number in passing without the question's context. So "the model ignored the context" is the main error here, and a bigger generator is the fix; with this model, better retrieval cannot raise accuracy much above 0.25. Twelve questions is a tiny set: one question is 0.08.

## Day 116: Quantisation from scratch (RTN int8/int4)
**Review today:** Day 115 (+1), Day 113 (+3), Day 109 (+7), Day 95 (+21; quick 15-min skim of its self-check).

### Block 1: Concept lesson (1h15)
**Why quantise?** LLM inference at small batch is limited by memory bandwidth: each generated token reads every weight. Storing weights in 8 or 4 bits instead of 32 or 16 cuts memory and, with suitable kernels, time. The cost is rounding error.

**Uniform quantisation.** For a group of weights w, choose a scale s and (optionally) a zero point z; store q = clamp(round(w/s) + z, qmin, qmax) and reconstruct ŵ = s·(q − z).
- *Symmetric*: z = 0, s = max|w| / (2^(b−1) − 1). Simple, good for roughly symmetric weights.
- *Asymmetric*: uses min and max, so the full integer range covers [min, max].
- *

Round-to-nearest (RTN)* is the simplest choice: each weight rounded independently.

**Granularity.** One scale for a whole matrix (*per-tensor*) is ruined by outliers: one large weight forces a large scale and all small weights round to zero. *Per-channel* (one scale per output row) and *group-wise* (one scale per g consecutive weights, e.g. 64) adapt to local ranges, at the cost of storing more scales. Group size must divide the row length: SmolLM2's 576-wide rows allow 32 or 64 but not 128.

**Measuring.** Relative weight error ‖W − Ŵ‖/‖W‖ is cheap but indirect; what matters is model quality, here perplexity on held-out text (Shakespeare validation, as in Week 15).

### Block 2: Worked example (45 min)
`code/week-17/day116_quant_rtn.py` quantises all 210 linear layers of SmolLM2-135M (10

6.2M weights; the tied embedding / lm_head stays fp32) and evaluates perplexity.

**Verified (out/day116_quant_rtn.log):** fp32 baseline perplexity **26.29**, linear weights 424.7 MB. Example outlier: layer 0 `down_proj` max|w| = 2.875 vs mean |w| = 0.1441 (20×).

| Scheme | Rel. weight error | Size (incl. scales) | Perplexity |
|---|---|---|---|
| int8 per-tensor | 0.0364 | 106.2 MB | 28.55 |
| int8 per-channel | 0.0085 | 106.5 MB | **26.50** |
| int4 per-tensor | 0.5832 | 53.1 MB | 1,561,367.93 |
| int4 per-channel | 0.1547 | 53.4 MB | 64.84 |
| int4 group-64 | 0.1128 | 56.4 MB | 36.89 |
| int4 group-32 | 0.1006 | 59.7 MB | 33.27 |
| int4 group-64 asymmetric | 0.0941 | 59.7 MB | 33.69 |
| int3 group-64 | 0.2623 | 43.1 MB | 231.67 |

Each evaluation took about 1 s. Reading: int8 per-chann

el is almost free (26.29 → 26.50) at a quarter of the memory. At 4 bits granularity decides everything: per-tensor destroys the model, per-channel doubles perplexity, group-32 costs about 7 points. Smaller groups and asymmetric zero points cost about 3 MB more for the scales and zero points. At 3 bits, RTN breaks down. Weight error predicts the order of the rows but not the size of the perplexity change.

### Block 4: Practice (1h)

2. Why does per-tensor int4 fail but per-channel survive?
3. What is the storage overhead of fp16 scales for group size 64 at int4?
4. Why can relative weight error mislead?

**Answers.** (1) s = 2.0/7 ≈ 0.286; q = round([0.35, −1.4, 0.875, 7]) = [0, −1, 1, 7]; ŵ ≈ [0, −0.286, 0.286, 2.0]: the small weights are badly represented. (2) Outliers in some rows set a huge global scale; per-row scales isolate them. (3) 16 bits per 64 weights = 0.25 bits per weight, about 6% on top of 4 bits. (4) Errors in some layers (or directions that align wi

th large activations) matter far more for the output than others.

## Day 117: GPTQ/AWQ concepts, plus a Rust/PyO3 int8 kernel
**Review today:** Day 116 (+1), Day 114 (+3), Day 110 (+7), Day 96 (+21; quick 15-min skim of its self-check).

### Block 1: Concept lesson (1h15)
**What we really want.** Not small weight error but small *output* error: minimise ‖XW − XŴ‖ over real inputs X. A few hundred to a few thousand calibration tokens give X.

**GPTQ (idea).** Quantise the weights of a layer one input-column at a time; after rounding a column, update the *remaining, not yet quantised* columns to compensate for the error, using the inverse of the Hessian H = XᵀX (+ damping). Weights that correlate with the rounded one absorb its error. It is a fast approximation of the classical Optimal Brain Surgeon idea, applied layer by layer. In the paper the inputs of

each layer are taken from the already-quantised previous layers; our version takes them once from the fp32 model (a simplification).

**AWQ (idea).** A small fraction of input channels carry large activations, and errors in the weights that multiply them dominate the output. AWQ scales those weight columns *up* by s = (mean |x|)^α before quantising, and divides the input by s (mathematically identity, foldable into the previous layer), so important weights get relatively finer rounding. α is chosen per layer by grid search on calibration output error. No weight updates, just scales.

**Kernels.** Low-bit weights only save time if a kernel reads the packed integers and computes with them. On CPU, the key costs are memory traffic and vectorisation; on GPU, dedicated kernels unpack int4 insid

e the matmul.

**Rust and PyO3.** PyO3 lets Rust functions be called from Python, maturin builds them into a wheel, the `numpy` crate gives zero-copy access to arrays, and rayon parallelises loops across threads.

### Block 2: Worked example (45 min)
`code/week-17/day117_gptq_awq.py`: 2,048 calibration tokens from Shakespeare *training* text (perplexity is on validation text); computing all Hessians took 1.9 s.

**Verified (out/day117_gptq_awq.log):**

| per-channel | GPTQ | 0.0048 | 44.31 | 14.1 s |
| group-64 | RTN | 0.0127 | 36.89 | |
| group-64 | AWQ-style (mean α 0.33) | 0.0077 | **3

1.17** | |
| group-64 | GPTQ | 0.0026 | 31.96 | 13.7 s |

## Day 118: Inference serving: KV cache, batching, speculative decoding, vLLM/llama.cpp overview
**Review today:** Day 117 (+1), Day 115 (+3), Day 111 (+7), Day 97 (+21; quick 15-min skim of its self-check).

### Block 1: Concept lesson (1h15)
**Prefill and decode.** Generation has two phases: *prefill* processes the whole prompt in parallel (compute-bound), and *decode* produces one token per step (memory-bound at small batch, because each step reads all weights for little compute).

**KV cache.** In causal attention, the keys and values of past tokens never change. Store them per layer; each decode step then computes Q, K, V only for the new token and attends to the cache, instead of re-running the whole sequence. Cost per step drops from O(t) full forwards' worth to one token's worth. T

he price is memory: 2 (K and V) × layers × KV heads × head dim × tokens × bytes. Grouped-query attention (GQA, used by SmolLM2) shrinks it by sharing K/V heads across query heads.

**Batching.** Decoding several sequences together reuses each weight read for several tokens, so total throughput rises until compute becomes the limit; per-sequence speed falls a little. *Continuous batching* lets sequences join and leave the batch at every step instead of waiting for the slowest one. *PagedAttention* (vLLM) stores the KV cache in fixed-size blocks, like virtual-memory pages, to avoid fragmentation and allow sharing prefixes.

**Speculative decoding.** A cheap *draft* model proposes γ tokens; the *target* model checks all of them in one forward pass and keeps the longest prefix it agrees with (

for greedy: matching argmax), plus one token of its own. Output is identical to the target's; the speed-up depends on the acceptance rate and on how cheap the draft is. A bad draft makes it slower.

**Engines (from their READMEs, not run here).**
- **vLLM** (`out/docs_vllm_README.md`): lists PagedAttention, continuous batching, chunked prefill, prefix caching, quantisation (FP8, INT8, INT4, GPTQ/AWQ, GGUF and others), speculative decoding (n-gram, suffix, EAGLE, DFlash) and an OpenAI-compatible API server; the paper is "Efficient Memory Management for Large Language Model Serving with PagedAttention". It is GPU-oriented and was not installed.
- **llama.cpp** (`out/docs_llama_cpp_README.md`): "Plain C/C++ implementation without any dependencies", 1.5- to 8-bit integer quantisation, Apple si

licon (Metal) and CUDA support, GGUF models (loadable with `-hf`), and an OpenAI-compatible server (`llama-server`). **Not built here**: the box has no `g++`, `cmake` or `make`. On a machine with a C++ toolchain, follow its README's build instructions.

### Answers
1. It averages token vectors (masked) into one vector; normalising makes dot product equal cosine similarity.
2. Section chunking: recall@5 0.71 (vs 0.62-0.64 for word windows).
3. Score = Σ 1/(k + rank) over retrievers; it uses only ranks, so no score calibration is needed.
4. It attends across query and document jointly; it needs one forward per pair, so it is too slow for whole-corpus search (about 200 ms for 20 pairs here).
5. Raised it from 0.40 to 0.50 (recall@5 0.64 → 0.81).

7. s = max|w| / (2^(b−1) − 1), q = clamp(round(w/s), −2^(b−1), 2^(b−1) − 1), ŵ = s·q.

## Day 121: MDPs, returns and Bellman equations
**Review today:** Day 120 (+1), Day 118 (+3), Day 114 (+7), Day 100 (+21; quick 15-min skim of its self-check).

### Block 1: Concept lesson (1h15)
Month 5 opens with reinforcement learning (RL). Until now every model learned from a fixed dataset of inputs and targets. In RL there is no dataset: an **agent** acts in an **environment**, gets a **reward** after each action, and must find behaviour that collects as much reward as possible over time. The data the agent sees depends on what it does, so exploring and learning are tied together.

The standard formal model is the **Markov decision process (MDP)**. It has a set of states S, a set of actions A, a transition function p(s', r | s, a) that gives the probability of landing in state s' with

reward r after taking action a in state s, and a discount factor γ between 0 and 1. "Markov" means that the next state depends only on the current state and action, not on the earlier history. If the history matters, you must put the parts that matter into the state.

An **episode** runs from a start state until a terminal state is reached. The **return** from time t is the discounted sum of future rewards: G_t = r_{t+1} + γ r_{t+2} + γ² r_{t+3} + … With γ < 1, rewards far in the future count less, and the sum stays finite even if an episode never ends. When every reward is −1, the return can never be below −1/(1−γ). With γ = 1 you need episodes that are guaranteed to end.

A **policy** π(a | s) gives the probability of each action in each state. The **state-value function** V^π(s) is the

expected return when you start in s and follow π. The **action-value function** Q^π(s, a) is the expected return when you take a in s first and follow π after that. These are the two objects that nearly every RL method estimates.

The **Bellman expectation equation** is a consistency condition. The value of a state equals the expected immediate reward plus the discounted value of the next state:
V^π(s) = Σ_a π(a|s) Σ_{s',r} p(s',r|s,a) [r + γ V^π(s')].
For a finite MDP this is a linear system: V = r_π + γ P_π V, so V = (I − γ P_π)^{-1} r_π. You can solve it exactly with a linear solve, or iteratively by sweeping the update until the values stop changing. That iterative version is **policy evaluation**, the first dynamic-programming method (Day 122).

The **Bellman optimality equation** re

places the average over actions with a maximum: V*(s) = max_a Σ p(s',r|s,a)[r + γ V*(s')]. This equation is not linear, and solving it is the subject of Day 122.

Three design choices matter in practice. First, the **reward** says *what* you want, not *how* to do it. A −1 per step reward means "finish fast". Second, **γ** is part of the problem definition: it changes which policy is best, not only how fast learning goes. Third, **stochastic transitions** (slipping) make good plans worth less, and they hurt some plans more than others.

4. Why does the γ = 0.99 value of state 7 (−16.96) sit far above its bound of −100? **Answer:** episodes end, usually long before di

scounting makes a difference.

### Extra notes
- Infinite horizon with γ < 1 and episodic with γ = 1 are both standard settings. Mixing them up gives values that never converge.
- Rewards can be scaled without changing the best policy, but a constant added to every reward does change behaviour in episodic tasks: it changes how much ending early is worth.

### Going deeper
Write out Q^π in terms of V^π, and V^π in terms of Q^π. Note that the second only needs π and not the model. That is

why model-free control (Day 123) learns Q and not V.

### Interview-style question (15 min)
"Your agent learns to loop forever instead of finishing the task. What do you check?" Good answer: the reward (are there positive rewards that can be collected again and again?), γ (with γ close to 1, small repeated rewards add up), the terminal conditions, and whether the state includes what the agent needs to know.

### Common mistakes
- Bootstrapping from a terminal state's value. A terminal state's value must be zero.
- Action orders that do not match between your code and a library. This course hit exactly that bug on Day 122.
- Reporting V(start) as a "success rate". It is a discounted expected return.

## Day 122: Dynamic programming: policy evaluation, value iteration and policy iteration
**Review today:** Day 121 (+1), Day 119 (+3), Day 115 (+7), Day 101 (+21; quick 15-min skim of its self-check).

### Block 1: Concept lesson (1h15)
**Dynamic programming (DP)** solves an MDP when you know the full model p(s', r | s, a). It is not learning from experience. It is planning, and it is the reference that every learning method is measured against this week.

**Policy evaluation** (Day 121) computes V^π for a fixed π. **Policy improvement** then makes π greedy with respect to V^π: in each state, pick the action with the highest one-step lookahead value, Σ p(s',r|s,a)[r + γV^π(s')]. The *policy improvement theorem* says the new policy is at least as good everywhere. **Policy iteration (PI)** a

lternates the two steps until the policy stops changing. A finite MDP has finitely many deterministic policies and each step improves, so PI stops, usually after only a handful of iterations.

**Value iteration (VI)** skips full evaluation. It applies the Bellman optimality update V(s) ← max_a Σ p[r + γV(s')] once per sweep, until the largest change is below a tolerance. Each sweep is cheap, but with γ close to 1 it needs many sweeps, because the update shrinks the error only by about a factor of γ per sweep.

In matrix form the model is T[s, a, s'] and R[s, a] (built by `_rl.model`, with transitions out of terminal states set to zero). One VI sweep is then `Q = R + γ T @ V; V = Q.max(1)`. That is a single tensor contraction, which is why tabular DP is so fast on a CPU.

DP has two hard li

mits. It needs the model, and it touches every state on every sweep. A table with 10^12 states does not fit in memory. Days 123-125 remove each limit in turn: sampling removes the need for a model, and function approximation removes the need for a table.

**FrozenLake** is the test bed. An agent crosses a frozen lake from S to G. H marks holes, which end the episode with reward 0. Reaching G gives reward 1. On the slippery lake, the agent moves in the intended direction or either perpendicular direction with probability 1/3 each. The optimal policy is often strange: it sometimes points *away* from the goal so that the only possible slips are safe ones.

### Block 2: Worked example (45 min)
`day122_dynamic_programming.py` builds our own FrozenLake table, compares it with gymnasium's, and ru

**Verified (out/day122_dynamic_programming.log):**
- 4x4 gridworld, optimal V after 4 sweeps: [0 −1 −2 −3], [−1 −2 −3 −2], [−2 −3 −2 −1], [−3 −2 −1 0]. That is minus the number of steps to the nearest corner.
- Our FrozenLake table equals gymnasium's: True, for both maps.
- Slippery FrozenLake (success is the greedy policy's success rate when run in gymnasium for 2,000 episodes):

| Map | γ | VI sweeps | VI time | PI iterations | PI time | V(start) | Success |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 4x4 | 0.9 | 145 | 0.8 ms | 6 | 0.9 ms | 0.069 | 0.733 |
| 4x4 | 0.99 | 571 | 2.8 ms | 7 | 0.2 ms | 0.542 | 0.741 |
| 8x8 | 0.9 | 158 | 2.0 ms | 10 | 0.5 ms | 0.006 | 0.596 |
| 8x8 | 0.99 | 662 | 7.8 ms | 9 | 0.5 ms | 0.415 |

0.632 |

- max|V_VI − V_PI| was 1e-9 or less in every case.
- Optimal 4x4 actions (γ 0.99; L = left, D = down, R = right, U = up): LUUU / LHLH / UDLH / HRDG. Note the "U" in the top row: pushing into the wall means you can only slip sideways, never into a hole.
- Non-slippery 4x4: V(start) 0.951 = 0.99^5, found in 7 sweeps.

Why success is not V(start): gymnasium cuts episodes off at 100 steps (logged), and V is discounted. With γ = 0.9, a slow, safe path is worth almost nothing (0.006), but it still succeeds about 60% of the time.

2. PI ran in fewer iterations, but each one solves a linear system. When does VI win? **Answer:** for large state spaces, where the O(S³) solve is too expensive and a cheap

approximate sweep is enough.
3. Why does a larger γ raise the success rate on 8x8 (0.596 to 0.632)? **Answer:** with a small γ, the agent cares less about a far-off goal and accepts riskier or more aimless moves. With γ 0.99, it pays to be patient and safe.

- An "in-place" (Gauss-Seidel) sweep uses new values straight away and usually converges in fewer sweeps.

Asynchronous DP updates only the states an agent actually visits. Taken to the l

### Interview-style question (15 min)
"You have the full model of a 1,000-state MDP. Would you use RL?" Good answer: no. Solve it with VI or PI in milliseconds, and use RL only when the model is unknown or the state space is too large.

- Letting terminal states keep receiving value.
- Using a convergence threshold on the policy in VI. Use one on V.
- Checking only V and never running the policy in the real environment.

## Day 123: Monte Carlo and TD learning; Q-learning vs SARSA
**Review today:** Day 122 (+1), Day 120 (+3), Day 116 (+7), Day 102 (+21; quick 15-min skim of its self-check).

### Block 1: Concept lesson (1h15)
Without a model you learn from samples. **Monte Carlo (MC)** prediction waits until the episode ends and moves V(s) towards the actual return G: V(s) ← V(s) + α (G − V(s)). The target is unbiased but noisy, because G is a sum of many random rewards.

**Temporal-difference learning, TD(0)**, updates after every step, using its own estimate of the next state: V(s) ← V(s) + α (r + γV(s') − V(s)). The quantity in brackets is the **TD error** δ. TD is biased (it bootstraps from estimates that may be wrong) but has much lower variance. It also works on episodes that never end. In practice,

TD often learns faster.

For **control**, learn Q(s, a) instead, so that you can act greedily without a model. The agent must also explore, usually **ε-greedy**: a random action with probability ε, and otherwise the best one.

- **SARSA** (on-policy) uses the action it will actually take next: target r + γQ(s', a'). It learns the value of the ε-greedy policy it is following, *including* its own random mistakes.
- **Q-learning** (off-policy) uses the best next action: target r + γ max_a Q(s', a). It learns the value of the greedy policy, even though it behaves ε-greedily.

**Cliff walking** shows the difference. A 4x12 grid has a cliff along the bottom edge: stepping off costs −100 and sends you back to the start, and every other step costs −1. The shortest path runs along the cliff edge. Q

-learning learns that path, but while exploring with ε = 0.1 it sometimes falls off. SARSA takes those exploration slips into account and learns a safer path further from the edge.

### Block 2: Worked example (45 min)
`day123_mc_td_qlearning.py` runs two experiments. The first is a 5-state random walk: start in the middle, reward +1 only for leaving on the right. Its true values are 1/6 … 5/6. The second is cliff walking, built from scratch in `_rl.cliff`.

**Verified (out/day123_mc_td_qlearning.log):** RMS error on the random walk, mean of 10 seeds:

| Method | α | After 10 episodes | After 50 | After 100 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| MC | 0.01 | 0.209 | 0.143 | 0.098 |
| MC | 0.03 | 0.178 | 0.099 | 0.099 |
| TD | 0.05 | 0.175 | 0.065 | 0.036 |
| TD | 0.1 | 0.128 | 0.062 | 0.058 |
| TD | 0.1

5 | 0.094 | 0.076 | 0.072 |

Every TD setting beats every MC setting by episode 50. A larger α learns faster at first and then levels off at a higher error. That is the noise floor of a constant step size, and MC α 0.03 shows it too, staying at 0.099.

Cliff walking (ε 0.1, α 0.5, 500 episodes, 10 seeds):

| Algorithm | Online return, episodes 1-50 | Episodes 401-500 | Time |
|---|---|---|---|
| Q-learning | −118.3 | −53.0 | 0.8 s |
| SARSA | −116.6 | −28.8 | 0.9 s |

- Greedy path returns per seed: Q-learning scored −13 in all 10 seeds (the optimal cliff-edge path).
- SARSA scored −17 in 8 seeds and −19 in 1, both safer and longer routes. The remaining seed scored −100: its greedy policy looped until the 100-step cap.

So Q-learning has the better *final greedy* policy but the worse *onli

ne* return. SARSA is better while exploring, but its greedy policy is not always valid. Both facts come from the same run.

2. Implement **Expected SARSA**, whose target is r + γ Σ_a π(a|s')Q(s', a), and add it to the cliff experiment.

### Block 4: Practice (1h)
1. Why is the MC target unbiased and TD's biased? **Answer:** G is a sample of the true return, while r + γV(s') uses a current estimate V(s') that may be w

rong.
2. Why is SARSA's online return better on the cliff? **Answer:** it learns values that include ε-exploration, so it keeps away from the edge where a random step is fatal.
3. If ε → 0, what does SARSA converge to? **Answer:** the optimal policy, the same as Q-learning (given enough exploration along the way).

### Extra notes
- n-step TD and TD(λ) interpolate between TD (n = 1) and MC (n = ∞).
- Q-learning's max causes **maximisation bias** when estimates are noisy. Double Q-learning fixes this, and Day 125's target network is a related idea.

### Going dee

per
Prove to yourself that TD(0) with a fixed batch of episodes converges to the value of the maximum-likelihood Markov model, while batch MC converges to the average observed returns. This is why TD uses the Markov structure better.

### Interview-style question (15 min)
"On-policy vs off-policy: which for a robot learning on real hardware?" Good answer: on-policy methods such as SARSA account for the robot's own exploration, which matters when mistakes are expensive. Off-policy methods can reuse old or logged data, which matters when data is expensive. Many real systems learn off-policy in simulation and then fine-tune carefully.

### Common mistakes
- Updating Q(s', ·) instead of Q(s, a).
- Using Q(s', a') after a terminal step. The target there is just r.
- Judging an algorithm on one

seed.

## Day 124: Function approximation: from tables to features
**Review today:** Day 123 (+1), Day 121 (+3), Day 117 (+7), Day 103 (+21; quick 15-min skim of its self-check).

### Block 1: Concept lesson (1h15)
A table has one entry per state and nothing carries over from one state to another. Real problems have continuous states (CartPole's four numbers) or far too many states to list. **Function approximation** represents V(s) ≈ v̂(s, w) or Q(s, a) ≈ q̂(s, a, w), with a weight vector w that is much smaller than the state space. Each update changes the value of many similar states at once. That is generalisation, the same idea as supervised learning in Months 2-3.

The prediction objective is the mean squared value error, weighted by how often each state is visited. **Gradient MC** treats th

e return G as a supervised target: w ← w + α (G − v̂(s,w)) ∇v̂(s,w). That is ordinary SGD, and it converges to a local optimum of this error.

**Semi-gradient TD** uses the target r + γ v̂(s', w) but treats it as a constant when taking the gradient. That is why it is called "semi". It is not true gradient descent on any objective. With linear features it still converges, but to the *TD fixed point*, which can be worse than the best possible approximation. It does usually converge faster.

With **linear** approximation, v̂ = wᵀφ(s), and the gradient is just the feature vector φ(s). Common features are:
- **State aggregation:** group states and give each group one weight. Tabular learning is the special case with one group per state.
- **Tile coding / coarse coding:** several overlapping gri

ds.
- **Random Fourier features:** φ(s) = cos(Ws + b), with W and b drawn at random. They are smooth and work like an RBF kernel. Their *bandwidth*, the scale of W relative to the state units, controls how far each update spreads.

For control, the same idea gives **semi-gradient Q-learning**: w_a ← w_a + α δ φ(s). Combining *function approximation*, *bootstrapping* and *off-policy* learning is called the **deadly triad**. Together these three can make learning diverge, and Day 125's DQN is largely a set of tricks against it.

### Block 2: Worked example (45 min)
`day124_function_approx.py` runs two experiments.

**(1)** A 1000-state random walk. Each step jumps up to 100 states left or right. Leaving on the left gives −1 and leaving on the right gives +1. The true V comes from a linear so

lve. Both methods use 10 aggregated groups of 100 states and 5,000 episodes.

**(2)** Linear semi-gradient Q-learning on gymnasium CartPole-v1, with 256 random Fourier features, a step size normalised by ‖φ‖², 300 episodes, and ε decaying from 1 to 0.01 over 150 episodes. The greedy policy is evaluated on 20 episodes, with 500 as the cap.

**Verified (out/day124_function_approx.log):**
- Gradient MC (α 5e-4): RMS error 0.061. Semi-gradient TD (α 2e-3): RMS error 0.131. The best possible with this aggregation is 0.053. MC gets close to the best approximation, and TD settles at its own biased fixed point. TD's weights (−0.71 … 0.70) are flatter than MC's (−0.85 … 0.81).
- A first run used step sizes 100x smaller and left the weights far from converged, with RMS errors of 0.364 and 0.414. It

is not kept as a result, but it is a useful warning: check convergence before you compare methods.
- CartPole, feature scale [2.4, 3.0, 0.21, 3.0] (the state bounds), α 0.01: this **failed** in all 3 seeds. The last 50 training episodes averaged 9.4-9.5 steps and greedy evaluation averaged 9.3-9.4, which is what you get by always pushing the same way.
- CartPole, feature scale [0.5, 0.5, 0.05, 0.5] (narrower, so the features are more local), α 0.1: greedy evaluation averaged **500.0 (the cap) in all 3 seeds**. The last 50 training episodes averaged 500.0, 433.0 and 500.0. Each seed took 1.5-2.0 s on CPU.

The only difference between failure and success was the feature bandwidth and the step size. Those two hyperparameters decide whether a linear method works.

### Block 3: Lab (2h)
1. Run

the script and reproduce the log.
2. Change the number of groups to 5, 20 and 50. Record the "best possible" error and the MC error. More groups gives a lower floor but slower learning.
3. Replace aggregation with polynomial features of s/1000, and compare.

### Block 4: Practice (1h)
1. Why is semi-gradient TD not true SGD? **Answer:** the target depends on w, but its gradient is ignored, so the update is not the gradient of any fixed loss.
2. Why did wide features fail on CartPole? **Answer:** with smooth features covering the whole state space, the values of nearby situations where different actions are needed get blurred together, s

o the greedy action ends up the same everywhere.
3. Why divide by φᵀφ? **Answer:** it makes α roughly "the fraction of the error corrected per step", whatever the feature scale (normalised LMS).

### Block 5: Review (1h)
Self-check: (a) write the gradient MC and semi-gradient TD updates for linear v̂; (b) name the three parts of the deadly triad; (c) explain the gap between 0.131 and 0.053; (d) explain why a single CartPole run that succeeds proves little.

### Extra notes
- Linear methods with good features are a strong baseline: fast, stable, and easy to inspect.
- Normalising the state (as in Month 2) matters just as much in RL.

### Going deeper
Look at least-squares TD (LSTD), which solves for the TD fixed point directly in one linear solve. It is the function-approximation counterpar

t of Day 121's exact solve.

### Interview-style question (15 min)
"Your linear Q-learner diverges. What do you try?" Good answer: a smaller or normalised step size, feature scaling, on-policy targets, or experience replay with a target network. Also check for a bug in the terminal-state target.

- Bootstrapping across episode truncation (time limit) as if it were termination, or the reverse. gymnasium returns them separately; use `terminated`, not `truncated`, to zero the target.
- Comparing methods before they have converged.

## Day 125: Deep Q-networks (DQN) on CartPole
**Review today:** Day 124 (+1), Day 122 (+3), Day 118 (+7), Day 104 (+21; quick 15-min skim of its self-check).

### Block 1: Concept lesson (1h15)
DQN is Q-learning with a neural network q̂(s, ·; θ) that outputs one Q-value per action. Feeding neural-network updates straight into Q-learning hits the deadly triad hard. Consecutive samples are strongly correlated, and the target r + γ max q̂(s', ·; θ) moves every time θ changes. DQN adds two stabilisers:

1. **Experience replay.** Store transitions (s, a, r, s', done) in a buffer, and train on random minibatches. This breaks correlations and reuses each sample many times, which makes learning more data-efficient.
2. **Target network.** Compute targets with a frozen copy θ⁻ and copy θ into θ⁻ eve

ry C steps. The regression target then stays fixed for a while, so each phase is close to supervised learning.

The loss is the Huber (smooth L1) loss between q̂(s, a; θ) and y = r + γ(1 − done) max_a' q̂(s', a'; θ⁻). It is optimised with Adam. Exploration is ε-greedy, with ε decaying over the first part of training.

Well-known extensions are **Double DQN** (choose the next action with θ and score it with θ⁻, which reduces maximisation bias), **dueling heads**, **prioritised replay** and n-step returns. They are worth knowing by name. This course does not implement them this week.

**CPU vs GPU.** CartPole's network is tiny (4-64-64-2), so a GPU would not speed it up. The time goes on Python environment steps and small-batch overheads. GPUs matter for DQN on images, such as Atari frames t

hrough a convolutional network, where each update is far larger.

### Block 2: Worked example (45 min)
`day125_dqn_cartpole.py` setup:
- Network: MLP 4-64-64-2.
- Replay buffer: 20k transitions; batch 64; Adam 1e-3; Huber loss.
- Target network synced every 500 steps.
- ε from 1 to 0.05 over 10k steps.
- 30k environment steps per seed; learning starts after 1k steps.
- Greedy evaluation: 20 episodes after every 10k steps.
- Ablation: no target network, where targets come from the online net.
- `torch.set_num_threads(1)`, because for a net this small more threads only add overhead.

**Verified (out/day125_dqn_cartpole.log):**

| Run | Training episodes | Mean length, last 20 | Greedy eval at 10k / 20k / 30k steps | Time |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Target net, seed 0 | 307 | 274.9 | 165.2 / **

500.0** / 176.8 | 18 s |
| Target net, seed 1 | 411 | 75.5 | 85.5 / 85.2 / 167.1 | 19 s |
| Target net, seed 2 | 332 | 249.8 | 102.6 / 177.9 / 116.7 | 18 s |
| No target net, seeds 0-2 | about 2,800 | 9.2-9.8 | 9.3-9.4 at every checkpoint | 17-18 s |

What this shows:
1. With a target network, DQN clearly learns, from about 9 steps to between 85 and 500. But it is **unstable**: seed 0 reached the 500 cap at 20k steps and then fell back to 176.8. This rise and collapse is the typical DQN behaviour, and it is why people keep the best checkpoint, judged on a separate evaluation.
2. Without a target network, all 3 seeds **collapsed** to the "always push one way" policy, the same failure as Day 124's badly scaled linear run.

## Day 126: PROJECT W18: model-free agents on FrozenLake 8x8 vs the DP optimum; Quiz 18
**Review today:** Day 125 (+1), Day 123 (+3), Day 119 (+7), Day 105 (+21; quick 15-min skim of its self-check).

### Block 1: Concept lesson (1h15)
The project question is: **how close do model-free learners get to the planning optimum, and how should we measure it?** On FrozenLake 8x8 (slippery, γ 0.99), DP gives the exact answer (Day 122), so learning can be scored against the truth. That is rarely possible in real problems.

There are three metrics, and each answers a different question:
1. **max Q(start) vs V*(start).** Has the agent learned the *values*? SARSA learns the value of its ε-greedy policy, so it should come out below V*.
2. **Policy agreement.** In what fraction of non-terminal states is

the greedy action optimal? Count an action as optimal if its one-step lookahead under V* equals the best one, so that ties are allowed.
3. **Greedy success in gymnasium.** How well does the policy actually do in the real environment, with its 100-step limit? Use 2,000 evaluation episodes with fixed seeds.

There is also one *online* metric: the success rate over the last 1,000 training episodes, with ε at 0.05. It is collected in our own environment, with a 200-step cap per episode. Because the cap is longer than gymnasium's 100 steps, online success can come out *higher* than greedy success in gymnasium. Always state the conditions behind a metric.

### Block 2: Worked example (45 min)
`day126_project.py` runs tabular Q-learning and SARSA from scratch: α 0.1, ε from 1 to 0.05 over 80% of

the episodes, random tie-breaking, 5,000 and 20,000 episodes, 3 seeds each. The 8x8 map has 64 states and 4 actions.

**Verified (out/day126_project.log):** DP optimum: V(start) 0.415; greedy success in gymnasium 0.643. This is 2,000 episodes with different seeds from Day 122, which measured 0.632 on the same policy, so the evaluation noise is about ±0.01.

| Q-learning, 5k | 0.391 / 0.382 / 0.409 | 79% / 77% / 81% | 0.611 / 0.552 / 0.513 | 0.645 / 0.600 / 0.649 | 4 s |

## Day 127: Policy gradients: REINFORCE and baselines
**Review today:** Day 126 (+1), Day 124 (+3), Day 120 (+7), Day 106 (+21; quick 15-min skim of its self-check).

### Block 1: Concept lesson (1h15)
**Why learn the policy directly?** Week 18 learned values (V, Q) and acted greedily on them. That works when actions are few and discrete and a max over them is cheap. Policy-gradient methods instead parameterise a stochastic policy π_θ(a|s), usually a softmax over network outputs, and climb the expected return J(θ) = E_τ~π_θ[G(τ)] directly. Advantages: they handle continuous or huge action spaces (a language model's vocabulary is the action space on Day 132), they can represent stochastic optimal policies, and small parameter changes give small behaviour changes instead of the sudden argmax

flips that destabilised DQN.

**The log-derivative trick.** We cannot differentiate through the environment, but we can differentiate the probability of the actions we took:

∇_θ J = E[ Σ_t ∇_θ log π_θ(a_t|s_t) · G_t ],

where G_t = Σ_k γ^k r_{t+k+1} is the return from step t onward. The environment dynamics drop out because they do not depend on θ. In code, you build the "surrogate loss" L = −Σ_t log π_θ(a_t|s_t)·G_t, with G_t treated as a constant, and call backward. Only rewards *after* step t multiply step t's log-probability ("reward to go"), because an action cannot affect the past; using the full-episode return is still unbiased but noisier.

**Variance is the enemy.** The estimator is unbiased but extremely noisy: one episode on CartPole can last 9 steps or 500, and every log-prob

ability in it is pushed by that return. On CartPole all rewards are +1, so every G_t is positive, and REINFORCE pushes up *every* action taken; it only learns because long episodes push harder.

**Baselines.** For any function b(s) that does not depend on the action, E[∇ log π(a|s)·b(s)] = b(s)·∇ Σ_a π(a|s) = b(s)·∇1 = 0. So we can subtract a baseline without adding bias: use (G_t − b(s_t)). A good b makes the weight positive for better-than-usual actions and negative for worse-than-usual ones, which cuts variance. Two common choices: a constant (the mean return), or a learned value network V_w(s) fitted by regression to G_t. The quantity G_t − V(s_t) is an estimate of the **advantage** A(s,a) = Q(s,a) − V(s), the central object of the rest of the week.

**Practical details.** Normalising

returns per batch is common but changes the effective step size; we keep raw returns and use Adam. Discount γ 0.99 makes the horizon about 100 steps. Evaluation uses the greedy policy (argmax) on 20 held-out seeds, because the stochastic training policy understates what the network knows.

- No baseline: mean episode length in episodes 1

-50 / 251-300 was 18.2 / 159.9 (seed 0), 25.6 / 89.8 (seed 1), 27.4 / 29.1 (seed 2); greedy eval 125.3, 176.6, 29.2.
- Value baseline: 19.4 / 218.6, 25.0 / 411.2, 30.9 / 368.2; greedy eval 127.0, 478.9, 308.8.
- Environment steps used: 17,397 / 19,571 / 8,383 without a baseline, 45,666-48,298 with one. Each seed ran in 1-4 s.

But note the confound: a fixed *episode* budget means better policies consume more *steps* (longer episodes), so the baseline runs also saw about 2-5 times more data. Day 133 fixes this by giving every method the same step budget. Seed 2 without a baseline never took off (29.1 at the end): a reminder that three seeds are a

minimum, not a proof.

## Day 128: Actor-critic (A2C)
**Review today:** Day 127 (+1), Day 125 (+3), Day 121 (+7), Day 107 (+21; quick 15-min skim of its self-check).

### Block 1: Concept lesson (1h15)
**From baseline to critic.** In REINFORCE with a baseline, V(s) only reduces variance; the target is still the full Monte Carlo return, so the agent must wait until the episode ends. Actor-critic methods use the value function *inside the target*. The one-step advantage estimate is the TD error

δ_t = r_{t+1} + γ V(s_{t+1}) − V(s_t),

and an n-step version sums n real rewards before bootstrapping: A_t ≈ r_{t+1} + γ r_{t+2} + … + γ^{n−1} r_{t+n} + γ^n V(s_{t+n}) − V(s_t). Small n means low variance but biased by the critic's errors; large n moves back towards Monte Carlo. This is the same bias-variance dial you met

we bootstrap through truncation and only zero the value on true termination. This is a small line of code with a large effect on stability.

**Why A2C is fragile.** The actor follows a critic that is itself learning, and the target moves with both. One bad step can push the policy into a region where episodes are short, the critic learns those, and the agent does not recover. You will see exactly that in the log.

## Day 129: PPO from scratch
**Review today:** Day 128 (+1), Day 126 (+3), Day 122 (+7), Day 108 (+21; quick 15-min skim of its self-check).

### Block 1: Concept lesson (1h15)
**The problem PPO solves.** A2C takes one gradient step per batch and throws the batch away. Taking many steps on the same batch would be more sample-efficient, but the policy-gradient estimate is only valid near the policy that collected the data. Push too far and the update is computed from data that no longer describes your policy, which is how runs collapse.

**Importance ratio.** Let π_old be the policy that collected the batch and r_t(θ) = π_θ(a_t|s_t) / π_old(a_t|s_t). At θ = θ_old the gradient of E[r_t·A_t] equals the ordinary policy gradient, so r_t·A_t is a surrogate objective we can optimise for several e

pochs.

**Clipping.** PPO (Schulman et al. 2017, https://arxiv.org/abs/1707.06347) maximises

L^CLIP = E[ min( r_t A_t, clip(r_t, 1−ε, 1+ε) A_t ) ].

Read the two cases. If A_t > 0, the objective stops increasing once r_t > 1+ε: no incentive to make a good action much more likely than before in one update. If A_t < 0, it stops once r_t < 1−ε. The min makes this a pessimistic bound: clipping can only remove incentive, never add it. It is a cheap stand-in for a trust region (a KL constraint between old and new policy), and you can monitor that KL directly.

**GAE.** PPO usually computes advantages with generalised advantage estimation: A_t = Σ_k (γλ)^k δ_{t+k}, where δ is the TD error from Day 128. λ = 0 is the one-step TD advantage; λ = 1 is the Monte Carlo advantage minus V. We use γ 0.99,

λ 0.95, and the recursion runs backwards over the rollout, resetting at true terminations.

**The full loop.** Collect T = 1024 steps with π_old; compute GAE and value targets (A + V); normalise advantages; for 10 epochs, shuffle into minibatches of 64 and step on policy loss + 0.5·value loss − 0.01·entropy, with gradient-norm clipping at 0.5 and Adam 3e-4; repeat until 50k steps. Diagnostics after each update: approximate KL between old and new policy, and the fraction of samples whose ratio left [0.8, 1.2].

### Block 2: Worked example (45 min)
Run `python code/week-19/day129_ppo.py` (about 30 s per seed). It trains with ε = 0.2 and then an ablation with no clipping (ε = 10^9: the same 10 epochs of plain importance-weighted policy gradient on each batch).

**Verified (out/day129_ppo.log

):**

Approximate KL per update: max 0.017-0.019, mean 0.006-0.007. About 0.06 of ratios were outside [0.8, 1.2]. 29-30 s per seed.
- **No clip:** 619, 456 and 624 episodes. KL max 2.432 / 2.790 / 2.352, mean 0.531 / 0.607 / 0.339; clip fraction 0.53 / 0.55 / 0.47; 26 s per seed. Evaluations kept collapsing: seed 0 fell to 10, 10, 10 at updates 44-46 before ending at 500; seed 1 ended at 121; seed 2 hit 39, 10, 14 at updates 45-47 and ended at 476.

**Reading it.** With clipping, the per-update KL stayed below 0.02 and all three seeds held 500 for the last ~17-20 upd

Without clipping, the KL per update was about 100 times larger and half the samples had moved outside the clip range; the policy repeatedly jumped to near-random behaviour (10 steps is roughly how long a falling pole lasts). The higher episode count for "no clip" is not a sign of learning more: short failed episodes inflate it. Wall-clock time is higher than A2C because of 10 epochs of minibatch updates, but the samples are used 10 times.

## Day 130: Exploration: bandits, UCB, Thompson sampling and a LinUCB recommendation tie-in
**Review today:** Day 129 (+1), Day 127 (+3), Day 123 (+7), Day 109 (+21; quick 15-min skim of its self-check).

### Block 1: Concept lesson (1h15)
**Bandits are RL with one state.** You repeatedly choose one of K arms; arm k pays a reward drawn from an unknown distribution with mean μ_k. There are no states to plan over, so the only difficulty is the **exploration-exploitation** trade-off. Performance is measured by **regret**: Σ_t (μ* − μ_{a_t}), the reward lost compared with always pulling the best arm.

**Strategies.**
- *Greedy:* pull the arm with the highest sample mean. It can lock onto a mediocre arm forever after a lucky start.
- *ε-greedy:* with probability ε pull a random arm. Simple, but

it keeps exploring at a fixed rate forever, so regret grows linearly.
- *Optimistic initial values:* start every estimate at the maximum possible reward (Q0 = 1 for Bernoulli). Each pull disappoints, so the agent tries everything early, then settles.
- *UCB1:* pull argmax_k Q_k + c·sqrt(2 ln t / N_k). The bonus shrinks as an arm is tried; this is "optimism in the face of uncertainty" with a guarantee of logarithmic regret.
- *Thompson sampling:* keep a Beta(α_k, β_k) posterior per arm, sample one value from each, pull the arm with the highest sample, update with the observed 0/1 reward. It explores exactly as much as the posterior is uncertain.

**Contextual bandits and recommendation.** In a recommender, each round you see a context x (user features), choose an item, and observe a click.

A contextual bandit learns a model of reward given context and item. **LinUCB** assumes reward ≈ θ_k·x for each item k, fits θ_k by ridge regression, and adds an uncertainty bonus α·sqrt(xᵀ A_k⁻¹ x). This is the same optimism idea as UCB1, with the count replaced by a covariance. Without context, a single "best item for everyone" policy cannot exploit the fact that different users like different things.

**Why this belongs in an RL week.** Every exploration idea in deep RL (entropy bonuses, optimism, posterior sampling, count-based bonuses) has its cleanest form here. And at LLM scale, sampling G answers per prompt and reinforcing the better ones (Day 132) is a bandit-like structure per prompt.

### Block 2: Worked example (45 min)
Run `python code/week-19/day130_bandits.py`. Part 1: a 10

## Day 131: Reward shaping pitfalls
**Review today:** Day 130 (+1), Day 128 (+3), Day 124 (+7), Day 110 (+21; quick 15-min skim of its self-check).

### Block 1: Concept lesson (1h15)
**Sparse rewards are slow.** If the only reward is +1 at the goal, an agent must stumble onto the goal by chance before anything is learned. A natural fix is **reward shaping**: add intermediate rewards that hint at progress. The danger is that the agent optimises the reward you wrote, not the goal you meant.

**The classic failure.** Reward the agent +0.1 every time it moves closer to the goal, and nothing for moving away. A loop "step closer, step back, step closer…" now earns 0.1 every two steps, forever. With γ = 0.99 that stream is worth about 0.1/(1−0.99²) ≈ 5, far more than the single +1 at the goal. T

he optimal policy for the shaped MDP is to never finish. This is **reward hacking** in miniature, and it is the same phenomenon Month 4 met when reward models were exploited by RLHF policies.

**Potential-based shaping.** Ng, Harada and Russell (1999) showed that if the shaping term has the form F(s, s') = γΦ(s') − Φ(s) for any function Φ of state, the optimal policy is unchanged. Intuition: along any path the terms telescope, so the total shaping bonus depends only on the start and end states, and loops earn exactly zero (minus discounting). You can encode a heuristic (here Φ = −0.1 × Manhattan distance) without creating a loophole. With Φ(goal) = 0, the shaped values are V'(s) = V(s) − Φ(s).

**But "preserves the optimal policy" is not "always faster".** Shaping changes the values the le

arner starts from and the paths it explores. A potential can help on average while still sending some runs down an unlucky road. Always measure.

### Block 2: Worked example (45 min)
Run `python code/week-19/day131_reward_shaping.py`. Setup: a deterministic 10x10 grid from (0,0) to (9,9), +1 on reaching the goal, γ 0.99, a 200-step cap. Two checks: (1) value iteration on each reward, and whether its greedy policy reaches the goal; (2) tabular Q-learning (α 0.5, ε 0.1, Q0 = 0), 10 seeds, recording the first episode at which the greedy policy follows an 18-step shortest path (within 1,000 episodes).

**Verified (out/day131_reward_shaping.log):**
- **Base reward:** the value-iteration policy reaches the goal in 18 steps. Q-learning first-success episodes: 70, 80, 58, 49, 53, 38, 63, 55, 53, 5

1; 10/10 seeds, median 54.
- **Naive shaping (+0.1 per step closer):** the value-iteration policy does **not** reach the goal (it loops). Q-learning: 0/10 seeds ever found the shortest path.
- **Potential-based (Φ = −0.1·distance):** the value-iteration policy reaches the goal in 18 steps. Q-learning: 2, 95, 4, 38, 2, 70, 3, none, 94, 73; 9/10 seeds, median 38.

**Reading it.** The naive reward did not just slow learning; it changed the optimal behaviour, so even exact dynamic programming learned to loop. Potential-based shaping kept the optimum, and four seeds solved it within 4 episodes, but the spread is huge (2 to 95) and one seed never got there in 1,000 episodes. The median improved (38 vs 54), yet a safe claim from 10 seeds is "faster on most runs, not reliably faster". The base rew

ard was the most consistent.

### Block 3: Lab (2h)
1. Add a penalty of −0.1 for moving away (so loops net zero, undiscounted). Does VI now reach the goal? Why is this close to, but not exactly, potential-based?
2. Try Φ = −0.5·distance and Φ = −0.01·distance; record median and failures.
3. Investigate the failed potential-based seed: print its greedy path at episode 1,000.
4. Write a short note: three real-world reward specifications that could be hacked the same way.

### Block 4: Practice (1h)
1. Write the potential-based shaping term.
2. Why does it not change the optimal policy?
3. Estimate the discounted value of the naive loop.
4. Why did VI fail under naive shaping, not just Q-learning?
5. What is the honest summary of the potential-based result?

**Answers.** 1) F = γΦ(s') − Φ(s).

2) Sums telescope; every policy's return shifts by the same −Φ(s0). 3) About 0.1/(1−γ²) ≈ 5 (versus 1 for finishing). 4) The optimum of the shaped MDP itself is to loop. 5) Median faster (38 vs 54), high spread, one seed in ten failed.

### Block 5: Review (1h)
Do your review days. Flashcards: reward hacking; potential-based shaping; telescoping; "policy-preserving ≠ faster".

### Extra notes
- Reward models in RLHF are learned shaping functions with no such guarantee, which is one reason RLHF keeps a KL penalty to a reference model (Day 132).
- Termination rewards and penalties are also shaping: a per-step −1 makes the agent want to end episodes, which can mean failing fast.

### Going deeper
Search for Ng, Harada and Russell, "Policy invariance under reward transformations" (ICML 1999),

and read the main theorem and its proof sketch.

### Interview-style question (15 min)
"Your agent maximises a shaped reward but ignores the real goal. How do you diagnose and fix it?" Evaluate on the true objective separately; look at trajectories, not just returns; replace ad-hoc bonuses with potential-based ones or remove them; and treat any learned reward as exploitable.

### Common mistakes
- Evaluating with the shaped reward instead of the true one.
- Rewarding progress without penalising regress.
- Claiming a speed-up from one or two seeds.

## Day 132: RL for LLMs, revisited: PPO with a KL penalty, GRPO and DPO
**Review today:** Day 131 (+1), Day 129 (+3), Day 125 (+7), Day 111 (+21; quick 15-min skim of its self-check).

### Block 1: Concept lesson (1h15)
**The mapping.** For a language model, the state is the prompt plus the tokens so far, an action is the next token, and a full answer is an episode. A reward model (or a checker, e.g. for maths answers) scores the finished answer. Everything below is stated only as far as it can be checked in the cited papers.

**RLHF with PPO (InstructGPT, https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.02155).** The pipeline is supervised fine-tuning, then a reward model trained on human rankings of several responses per prompt (the paper uses K = 4 to 9 responses), then PPO against that reward. The paper add

s a per-token KL penalty from the SFT model to the reward, to stop the policy drifting into text that fools the reward model, and initialises the value function from the reward model. A variant, "PPO-ptx", also mixes in pretraining gradients. The DeepSeekMath paper describes the same set-up as the reward r_t = r_φ − β·log(π_θ/π_ref) per token, citing Ouyang et al. 2022. This is Day 128-129's PPO with Day 131's lesson built in: the learned reward is exploitable, so the KL term is a leash.

**The objective being approximated.** Maximising E[r] − β·KL(π‖π_ref) has the closed-form solution π*(y) ∝ π_ref(y)·exp(r(y)/β). You derived and computed this on Day 106; the DPO paper (https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.18290) uses it as its starting point.

**DPO.** Rearranging the closed form gives r(y) = β·lo

g(π*(y)/π_ref(y)) + β·log Z. Substituting into the Bradley-Terry preference model makes Z cancel, so the policy can be fitted directly to preference pairs with a logistic loss on β·(log-ratio of the winner − log-ratio of the loser). The paper's stated advantage is eliminating the need to sample from the LM during fine-tuning: it is offline, with no reward model and no PPO loop. You implemented it on Day 108.

**GRPO (DeepSeekMath, https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.03300).** The paper describes GRPO as a variant of PPO that drops the critic and instead estimates the baseline from group scores. For each question, sample a group of G outputs, score them, and give each output the advantage (r_i − mean(r)) / std(r); with outcome rewards that advantage is applied to every token of the output. The clipp

ed ratio objective is kept. Instead of putting KL in the reward, GRPO adds β·KL to the loss, using the estimator π_ref/π − log(π_ref/π) − 1, which the paper notes is guaranteed to be positive. Reported settings include policy learning rate 1e-6, KL coefficient 0.04 and 64 samples per question. The paper also frames SFT, rejection-sampling fine-tuning, DPO, PPO and GRPO in one "unified paradigm" that differs in data source and gradient coefficient, and reports that RL improved Maj@K but not Pass@K in its experiments.

**Connections to this week.** GRPO's group mean is Day 127's constant baseline, estimated per prompt; dropping the critic saves a model the size of the policy, which matters at LLM scale. Its group of samples per prompt is a bandit (Day 130) per prompt. The KL leash is the def

ence against Day 131's reward hacking.

### Block 2: Worked example (45 min)
Run `python code/week-19/day132_rl_for_llms.py` (about 4 s). It is a one-prompt "LLM" with five possible answers, reusing Day 106's numbers: rewards [1.0, 0.8, 0.5, 0.2, 0.0], π_ref = [0.05, 0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.35], β = 0.2. The policy is a softmax over five logits initialised at log π_ref, trained with Adam (lr 0.05) for 400 iterations, three seeds. Methods: REINFORCE with KL in the reward (64 samples, batch-mean baseline); PPO-clip with KL in the reward (4 epochs, ε 0.2); GRPO (8 groups of 8, group-normalised advantage, clipped, k3 KL in the loss with coefficient β); DPO (64 pairs per iteration sampled from π_ref, labelled by Bradley-Terry with the true rewards).

**Verified (out/day132_rl_for_llms.log):**
- Closed

form π* = [0.45, 0.331, 0.148, 0.049, 0.021]; reward 0.799; KL to ref 1.193 (matches Day 106). π_ref has reward 0.290 and total-variation (TV) distance 0.631 to π*.
- REINFORCE+KL and PPO-clip+KL, all three seeds: π = [0.45, 0.331, 0.148, 0.049, 0.021], TV 0.000, reward 0.799, KL 1.193.
- GRPO: π ≈ [0.921, 0.013, 0.018, 0.021, 0.027] (seed 0), TV 0.476 / 0.478 / 0.463, reward 0.945 / 0.943 / 0.925, KL 2.490 / 2.492 / 2.363.
- DPO: TV 0.060 / 0.080 / 0.033, reward 0.796 / 0.794 / 0.815, KL 1.185 / 1.179 / 1.282 (seed 1: π = [0.391, 0.388, 0.172, 0.034, 0.016]).

**Reading it.** Both on-policy methods with KL in the reward land exactly on the closed-form optimum, which confirms they optimise E[r] − β·KL. DPO, trained only on offline pairs from π_ref, gets close (TV 0.03-0.08); the remaining

error is noise from a fixed learning rate on sampled pairs, visible in seed 1 swapping the top two answers' masses. GRPO does **not** converge to the same π*: it reached higher reward and roughly double the KL. Two reasons follow from its definition, not from any claim in the paper: dividing by the group std rescales the reward, so the effective trade-off against the KL term is not the same β; and once most groups contain the same answer, their std is near zero and their advantage is zero, so only the KL term acts on them. The takeaway is not "GRPO is wrong" but that **β is not portable between methods**; the same number means a different leash.

### Block 3: Lab (2h)

2. Change the group size to 4

and 32.
3. Put GRPO's KL into the reward instead of the loss. Compare.
4. Halve DPO's learning rate (or decay it) and check whether TV falls.
5. Write a paragraph: which of these four would you choose at LLM scale with one GPU, and why (memory for policy, reference, value and reward models; online sampling cost).

### Block 4: Practice (1h)

3. In GRPO, where does it go and which estimator is used?
4. What does GRPO use instead of a critic?
5. Why does DPO not need sampling during training?

**Answers.** 1) π* ∝ π_ref·exp(r/β). 2) Into the per-token reward, as −β·log(π/π_ref). 3) Into the loss, with π_ref/π − log(π_ref/π) − 1. 4) The mean (and std) of rewards in a group of samples for the sam

e prompt. 5) It fits the policy directly to fixed preference pairs through the closed-form relation between reward and policy.

### Block 5: Review (1h)
Do your review days, especially Day 111's self-check. Flashcards: closed-form optimum; KL in reward vs in loss; group-relative advantage; k3 estimator; DPO's implicit reward; "β is not portable".

## Day 134: The agent loop and tool calling with JSON schemas
**Review today:** Day 133 (+1), Day 131 (+3), Day 127 (+7), Day 113 (+21; quick 15-min skim of its self-check).

### Block 1: Concept lesson (1h15)
**What an "agent" is, in one loop.** Strip the marketing away and an LLM agent is a while-loop around a model:

1. **Observe:** build a context from the task, the history so far and the tool descriptions.
2. **Think/decide:** ask the policy (the model) for the next action. That is either a *tool call* `{"tool": name, "args": {...}}` or a *final answer*.
3. **Act:** if it is a tool call, the *harness* (your code, not the model) validates it, runs it, and appends the result to the history as an observation.
4. Repeat until a final answer arrives or a step limit is hit.

The model never

executes anything itself. It only emits text. Every capability and every danger sits in what your harness agrees to run. That one sentence explains most of this week, including the safety material on Days 137 and 139.

**Why tools at all?** Week 17 showed that a 135M model cannot be trusted with facts or arithmetic. A tool turns "remember the population of Corvo" into "call `lookup`", and "divide two large numbers" into "call `calculator`". The model's job shrinks to *choosing* the action and *filling in its arguments*. On Day 135 we measure whether even that shrunken job is within reach of SmolLM2.

**Tool specification = name + description + JSON Schema.** Each tool is described to the model by a name, a natural-language description and a schema for its arguments. The verified MCP docs

use exactly this shape: a tool has a `name`, a `title`, a `description` and an `inputSchema` (JSON Schema). Our `tool_specs()` emits `{name, description, inputSchema}` so the format matches. The schema does two jobs. First, it goes into the prompt so the model knows what to produce. Second, the harness uses it as a contract to **validate before executing**. A schema like

`{"type":"object","properties":{"city":{"type":"string"},"field":{"type":"string","enum":["population","country","temp_c"]}},"required":["city","field"],"additionalProperties":false}`

rejects a missing field, a wrong type, an unknown enum value and any extra key. jsonschema is not installed in our venv, so `_agent.validate` implements the subset we need from scratch: type, enum, minimum/maximum, required, properties, add

itionalProperties and items. It is about 20 lines.

**Errors are observations.** When validation or execution fails, the harness does not crash. It returns `('error', message)` and appends the message to the history so the policy can correct itself. Good error messages are *for the model*: "$.field: 'area' not in ['population','country','temp_c']" tells it exactly what to change.

**Three tools in `_agent.py`.**
- `calculator(expression)` parses the expression with Python's `ast` module and allows only numbers and arithmetic operators, with a cap on exponents. It never calls `eval`. `open('x').read()` is rejected as "disallowed syntax: Call".
- `lookup(city, field)` reads a fictional six-city table (Avalon, Brindle, Corvo, Dunmere, Elsby, Farrow). The cities are invented so that the model

cannot already "know" the answers.
- `send_email(to, body)` is a *side-effect* tool. It only appends to an in-memory `OUTBOX` list and never sends anything. Tools carry a `side_effect` flag that Day 139 uses.
